lesson.title: Kubernetes from Zero, part 18: taints, priority and disruption budgets
lesson.description: Keep Pods off nodes with taints, let important Pods push others aside with PriorityClass, and drain a node safely behind a PodDisruptionBudget.
lesson.tested: Every command ran on a four-node kind v0.33.0 cluster (node v1.37.0, kubectl v1.37.2) on 10 Nov 2026
lesson.rule: Taint nodes to reserve them, give critical Pods a higher priority, and put a PodDisruptionBudget on every replicated app before anyone drains a node.

cheatsheet.intro: Taints, priority, budgets, and the commands from Lesson 18.

rows.name: Taint and toleration
rows.role: A taint keeps Pods off a node. A toleration lets a Pod in but does not pull it there. NoExecute also evicts running Pods.

rows.name: PriorityClass
rows.role: A cluster-wide object with a value up to 1 billion. Higher wins. A Pod without priorityClassName gets 0 unless a class is globalDefault. When the cluster is full, the scheduler can preempt lower-priority Pods.

rows.name: PodDisruptionBudget
rows.role: Limits how many replicas planned maintenance may take down at once. Only tools that use the Eviction API, such as kubectl drain, respect it.

rows.name: Cordon
rows.role: Mark the node unschedulable so new Pods are not placed there. Drain does this too.

rows.name: Drain
rows.role: Evict Pods, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets. Pass --ignore-daemonsets when DaemonSet Pods are present.

rows.name: Uncordon
rows.role: Tell the scheduler it may place Pods on the node again.

rows.name: tolerationSeconds
rows.role: With NoExecute, a Pod that tolerates the taint stays for this many seconds, then is evicted.

rows.name: Patch a budget
rows.where: the lab lowered minAvailable so drain could finish

items.what: The control-plane node already carries node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule, which is why ordinary Pods stay off it.
The event named batch-5bd8dd9495-mw2hl, preempted on k8s-ep16-worker3 so checkout could run there.
The refused drain said it would violate the pod's disruption budget. Lower the budget, or scale up. Do not delete the PDB in a hurry.
The lesson prefers maxUnavailable 1 over minAvailable N, because it still allows a disruption after a scale.

homework.intro: Use the three-worker kind cluster from part 17 and the namespace k8s-from-zero. Lab output uses the prefix k8s-ep16. Answers are in the separate answer key.

sections.title: Recall
sections.hint: Answer from memory, then check the lesson.

exercises.q: What is the difference between NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule and NoExecute?
exercises.a: NoSchedule blocks new Pods that do not tolerate the taint; Pods already running stay. PreferNoSchedule is a soft preference. NoExecute also evicts running Pods that do not tolerate the taint, immediately unless they set tolerationSeconds.

exercises.q: What range of values may a PriorityClass use, and what are the two built-in classes for?
exercises.a: Your classes can use any 32-bit integer up to 1 billion. Kubernetes ships system-cluster-critical and system-node-critical above that range for parts of the cluster itself. A Pod without priorityClassName gets priority 0, unless one class has globalDefault: true.

exercises.q: What does a PodDisruptionBudget limit, and which tools respect it?
exercises.a: It limits how many replicas of a matching app planned (voluntary) disruptions may take down at once. Only tools that use the Eviction API, such as kubectl drain, respect it. Deleting a Deployment or a Pod directly bypasses it.

exercises.q: Taint a worker with NoExecute and watch a Pod that has no toleration and one with tolerationSeconds: 20. What happens?
exercises.a: The Pod without a toleration is evicted immediately. The Pod that sets tolerationSeconds: 20 stays for about 20 seconds and is then evicted. After you remove the taint with a trailing hyphen, the node accepts Pods again.

exercises.q: Apply a low-priority batch Deployment and a higher-priority checkout Pod that needs more CPU than is free. What does the lesson show?
exercises.a: The scheduler preempts lower-priority batch Pods to place checkout. A FailedScheduling event may appear first while it looks for victims. Preemption is best-effort about PodDisruptionBudgets, and victims get their normal graceful termination period.

exercises.q: Apply a three-replica Deployment and a PDB with minAvailable that blocks drain, then patch the budget. What does drain do?
exercises.a: The first drain hits the budget and times out; the node may already be SchedulingDisabled. After patching minAvailable so one disruption is allowed, drain can evict a Pod and finish. Uncordon returns the node to Ready.

sections.title: Predict the outcome
sections.hint: Write your prediction first. Then check the answer key.

exercises.q: You taint a node NoSchedule but a Pod is already running there. Does it leave?
exercises.a: No. NoSchedule only blocks new Pods. Running Pods stay until you use NoExecute, drain the node, or delete them.

exercises.q: You delete a Deployment that has a PodDisruptionBudget. Does the budget stop the delete?
exercises.a: No. Deleting the Deployment bypasses the budget. PDBs apply to voluntary evictions through the Eviction API, such as kubectl drain.

exercises.q: A high-priority Pod stays Pending even after preemption. What cause does the lesson name?
exercises.a: Preemption only frees resources counted by requests. A node that looks busy but has low requests is not full to the scheduler. Also a class with preemptionPolicy: Never will not evict anybody.
